title: Incident command and communication
description: Learn about Incident command and communication. Master the concepts, patterns, and best practices.

data.text: **Incident command and communication** are the non-technical skills that separate good engineers from great leaders. This lesson teaches you how to run an incident war room, keep stakeholders informed, and make clear decisions under pressure.
The Incident Commander Role

The incident commander is the single person responsible for coordinating the response. They do not perform the technical investigation unless the team is small. They assign tasks, set priorities, make go or no-go decisions, and communicate to leadership. The commander must remain calm, process-oriented, and focused on the big picture. When the team is in chaos, the commander is the anchor.

terms.definition: The single point of accountability for the incident response process.
A dedicated communication space for incident responders.
The person who documents the timeline and decisions in real time.
The person responsible for all internal and external status updates.
Anyone who needs to know about the incident: leadership, legal, PR, customer success.

data.title: Senior Engineer Mindset
data.text: The incident commander should be the calmest person in the room. If the commander is panicking, the team will panic. Practice breathing techniques and decision frameworks before you need them.
Command Staff Roles

Every incident needs a command staff with clear roles. The **incident commander** owns the process. The **technical lead** owns the investigation. The **communications lead** owns internal and external updates. The **scribe** owns the timeline and postmortem draft. Assign these roles at the start of every SEV-1 and SEV-2 incident. Do not assume roles will emerge naturally.

rows: Coordinate response, assign tasks, make decisions
Status updates, status page, stakeholder briefings

data.text: Incident Command Decision-Making

Decision-making under pressure requires a framework. Use OODA: observe the situation, orient yourself with the data, decide on a course of action, and act. The cycle should be fast: observe for two minutes, orient for three minutes, decide for one minute, act for five minutes. Reassess after each action. Do not get stuck in analysis paralysis.

items: Observe: gather data from dashboards, alerts, and user reports
Orient: understand the blast radius, severity, and likely cause
Decide: choose a mitigation strategy with the technical lead
Act: execute the decision and monitor the result
Reassess: repeat the cycle until the incident is resolved

data.text: OODA Loop in Incident Response

The OODA loop was developed by military strategist John Boyd and is equally applicable to incident response. Observe the current state of the system, orient yourself by comparing it to known baselines, decide on the best course of action, and act quickly. The team that cycles through OODA faster than the incident evolves wins.

data.title: OODA Loop for Incident Response
data.content: Apply the OODA loop to every incident decision. Time-box each phase to prevent analysis paralysis.

data.text: Communication Principles

Communication during incidents follows three principles: be timely, be accurate, and be empathetic. Timely means posting updates at the promised interval even if there is no progress. Accurate means stating only confirmed facts. Empathetic means acknowledging user impact and avoiding technical jargon when talking to non-engineers.

items: Timely: post updates at the promised interval
Accurate: state only confirmed facts, not speculation
Empathetic: acknowledge user impact and avoid jargon
Consistent: use the same format for every update
Transparent: share what is being done and why

data.text: Status Update Format

Every status update should follow a consistent format: what happened, what is being done, and the expected next update. Keep it to three sentences. Pin it to the incident channel. Use bold text for the severity and estimated resolution time. This format is easy to scan under pressure.

data.title: Status Update Template
data.content: Use this template for every status update. It ensures consistency and scannability.
data.code:
STATUS_UPDATE_TEMPLATE = """
**[SEV-1] Payment Service Outage**

**What happened:** 40% of checkout attempts failing due to payment gateway timeout.

**What we are doing:** Rolling back last deployment to restore service.

**Next update:** 15 minutes.
"""

data.text: Internal Communication

Internal communication keeps the team aligned and prevents rumor mills. The incident commander should post updates to the incident channel every 15 minutes for SEV-1 and every 30 minutes for SEV-2. The communications lead should keep a separate channel for leadership updates. Avoid broadcasting technical details to the entire company unless the incident is SEV-1.

items: Incident channel: real-time updates for responders
Leadership channel: summarized updates for executives
Engineering all-hands: brief mention if SEV-1
Company-wide: only if the incident affects all users

data.text: External Communication

External communication shapes customer trust. The status page is the primary channel. Update it within 15 minutes of declaring the incident. Use plain language. Say some users cannot complete checkout, not we are experiencing elevated 502 errors in the payment service. Provide an estimated resolution time when known and update the page regularly.

data.title: Plain Language
data.text: Never use internal jargon on the status page. Customers do not know what a 502 error is. They know that they cannot buy products.
Status Page Writing

Status page updates should be short, factual, and forward-looking. Include what happened, what is being done, and the expected timeline. End with a statement of commitment: we are working to resolve this as quickly as possible. Do not make promises you cannot keep. If the ETA is uncertain, say we are investigating and will provide an update within 30 minutes.

items: State the problem in plain language
Provide an ETA or an update commitment
Update the page at the promised interval

data.text: Customer Support During Incidents

Customer support is on the front line during incidents. They receive the tickets, the calls, and the angry tweets. Equip them with a one-sentence summary they can share. Loop them into the incident channel for real-time updates. Brief them every 30 minutes so they can answer customer questions accurately.

items: Provide a one-sentence summary to customer support
Loop support into the incident channel as observers
Provide support with a canned response they can adapt

data.text: Executive Communication

Executives need a different level of detail than engineers. Focus on business impact: revenue at risk, user count affected, and expected resolution time. Do not show them stack traces. Use analogies: the payment gateway is a dam and we are patching the leak. Brief the CEO or VP directly for SEV-1 incidents affecting revenue.

data.title: Executive Briefing
data.text: For SEV-1 incidents, brief the CEO within 30 minutes. Focus on revenue impact, user count, and resolution plan. Do not include technical details.
Media and PR Communication

Media inquiries during incidents require careful handling. The communications lead should be the single point of contact for all press. Prepare a holding statement in advance. Do not speculate about root cause. Do not promise specific resolution times. Acknowledge the issue, state that the team is investigating, and commit to providing more information when available.

items: Prepare a holding statement template in advance
Route all media inquiries through the communications lead
Acknowledge the issue without speculating on cause
Commit to providing updates without promising timelines

data.text: Legal and Compliance Communication

Legal and compliance teams must be informed early for incidents with regulatory implications. Data breaches, privacy violations, and financial reporting errors all require legal review. The incident commander should loop in legal counsel within one hour of identifying a compliance risk. Legal will advise on notification requirements and evidence preservation.

items: Notify legal within 1 hour for compliance-related incidents
Preserve evidence for potential litigation or regulatory investigation
Coordinate with legal on public statements

data.text: Board and Investor Communication

For incidents with material business impact, the board or investors may need to be informed. The CEO should prepare a brief factual summary: what happened, the business impact, the resolution timeline, and the steps being taken to prevent recurrence. Avoid technical details and focus on financial and reputational impact.

data.title: Board Communication
data.text: For material incidents, brief the board within 24 hours. Provide a factual summary with financial impact and remediation steps. Reserve detailed technical analysis for the postmortem.
Incident Command Handoffs

In a follow-the-sun on-call model, incident commanders may change shifts during a long incident. The handoff should be explicit and documented. The outgoing commander should brief the incoming commander on the current status, the actions taken, the remaining budget, and the next steps. Use a handoff template to ensure nothing is missed.

data.title: Incident Commander Handoff Template
data.content: Use this template when transferring incident command to the next on-call shift.
data.code:
HANDOFF_TEMPLATE = {
    "incident_id": "INC-2024-001",
    "severity": "SEV-1",
    "current_status": "Mitigated, monitoring for regression",
    "actions_taken": ["Rolled back deploy", "Killed feature flag"],
    "remaining_budget": "5 percent",
    "next_steps": ["Verify recovery", "Write postmortem"],
    "open_questions": ["Root cause still unknown"],
    "stakeholders_updated": ["CEO", "customer success"],
    "status_page_status": "Resolved"
}

data.text: Incident Command Across Time Zones

Global teams need incident command that spans time zones. Define an escalation policy that ensures a commander is always available. Use async handoff documents and overlapping shifts. The commander in the active time zone makes operational decisions; the on-call in the next time zone takes over at the shift boundary.

items: Define overlapping on-call shifts of at least two hours
Use async handoff documents with full incident context
Escalate to the next time zone commander at shift boundary
Record war room sessions for asynchronous review

data.text: Incident Command and Psychological Safety

The incident commander sets the tone for the entire response. A commander who blames, raises their voice, or panics creates a toxic war room. A commander who remains calm, asks questions, and values every contribution creates a team that performs under pressure. Explicitly state at the start of every incident that this is a blameless response.
The incident commander is the thermostat, not the thermometer. They set the temperature of the room.
Incident Command Training

Incident command is a skill that must be trained, not assumed. Provide formal training that covers decision-making frameworks, communication techniques, and stress management. Run tabletop exercises where engineers practice being incident commanders. Rotate the role so that multiple engineers gain experience.

items: Provide formal incident command training for all senior engineers
Rotate the incident commander role among on-call engineers
Debrief after each exercise to identify improvement areas

data.text: Incident Command Metrics

Track incident command performance alongside technical metrics. Measure the time from incident declaration to first status update, the consistency of update intervals, and the time from detection to stakeholder briefing. Use these metrics in incident command training and performance reviews.

rows: Stops rumor mills and reduces stakeholder anxiety
Shows professionalism and keeps stakeholders informed
Shows commitment to learning and accountability

data.text: Incident Command and Emotional Intelligence

Emotional intelligence is as important as technical skill during incidents. The commander should read the room, recognize when team members are stressed, and adjust the pace accordingly. They should de-escalate conflicts, credit contributions, and maintain morale. An incident that ends with the team feeling supported is more likely to result in honest postmortems and long-term improvements.

items: Read the room and adjust the pace to team capacity
De-escalate conflicts before they disrupt the response
Credit contributions publicly to build morale
Check in with stressed team members privately

data.text: Incident Command and Delegation

The incident commander must delegate effectively. Do not try to do everything yourself. Assign a technical lead for investigation, a communications lead for updates, and a scribe for documentation. Trust your team to execute. Check in regularly but do not micromanage. Micromanagement during incidents slows the team down and erodes trust.

data.title: Micromanagement Risk
data.text: The incident commander should not perform technical investigation unless the team is small. Delegation is a force multiplier. Trust your team.
Incident Command and Decision Records

Every significant decision during an incident should be recorded in the timeline. Include the decision, the alternatives considered, the rationale, and the outcome. Decision records make the postmortem factual and protect the team from hindsight bias. They also help the team learn which decision frameworks work best under pressure.

data.title: Decision Record Format
data.content: Record every significant decision in the incident timeline. This makes the postmortem factual and supports organizational learning.
data.code:
DECISION_RECORD = {
    "timestamp": "2024-01-15T14:08:00Z",
    "decision": "Roll back deployment",
    "alternatives": ["Hotfix", "Feature flag kill", "Wait for fix"],
    "rationale": "Rollback is fastest and safest. Feature flag not available for this change.",
    "outcome": "Service restored in 4 minutes"
}

data.text: Incident Command and Crisis Communication

For existential crises such as data breaches or complete platform outages, the incident commander must coordinate with the crisis management team. The commander provides technical updates, the crisis team makes strategic decisions. The commander should prepare a one-page technical summary for the crisis team every hour.

items: Prepare a one-page technical summary for the crisis team
Coordinate with legal counsel on communication content
Avoid speculation in any public or internal statement
Document all decisions for potential litigation

data.text: Incident Command and Post-Incident Review

After the incident, the commander should participate in the postmortem and reflect on their own performance. What decisions were correct? What could have been faster? Did the team have the information they needed? The commander should solicit feedback from the team and use it to improve. The best incident commanders are lifelong learners.

items: Solicit feedback from the team on command performance
Identify one area for improvement in the next incident
Document lessons learned in the incident knowledge base

data.text: Incident Command and Tooling

The right tools make incident command easier. Use an incident management platform that supports role assignment, timeline tracking, and status page integration. Ensure the commander has access to dashboards, the incident channel, and the status page on a single screen. Use a second monitor if possible. The goal is to see everything without switching contexts.

data.title: Commander Dashboard
data.text: Set up a commander dashboard that shows the incident timeline, status updates, SLI burn rate, and stakeholder list on a single screen. Reduce context switching during high-stress incidents.
Incident Command and Decision Fatigue

Decision fatigue is real during long incidents. The commander should take breaks, eat, and stay hydrated. Delegate decisions to the technical lead when possible. If the incident is expected to last more than four hours, rotate the commander role. A tired commander makes worse decisions.

items: Take a 10-minute break every two hours
Rotate the commander role for incidents longer than 4 hours
Delegate non-critical decisions to the technical lead

data.text: Incident Command and Stakeholder Management

Stakeholders include executives, legal, PR, customer success, and board members. Each group needs different information at different frequencies. The communications lead should maintain a stakeholder map with contact details, information needs, and update frequencies. Brief stakeholders proactively so they do not demand information during the incident.

data.title: Stakeholder Communication Map
data.content: Define who needs what information and how often. This prevents the incident team from being interrupted by ad-hoc requests.

data.text: Incident Command and Remote Collaboration

Remote incident command requires intentional tooling and process. Use video calls for the war room so facial expressions and body language are visible. Share screens for dashboards. Use a shared document for the timeline. Mute microphones when not speaking to reduce noise. Ensure every participant has a stable internet connection and a backup such as a mobile hotspot.

items: Use video calls for the war room
Use a shared document for the timeline

data.text: Incident Command and Accessibility

Incident response tools and runbooks should be accessible to all engineers, including those with disabilities. Use screen-reader-friendly formats, closed captions for video calls, and keyboard-navigable dashboards. Include accessibility requirements in runbook design reviews. An inaccessible incident response process excludes engineers and reduces team effectiveness.

data.title: Accessibility
data.text: Test runbooks and dashboards with screen readers. Include closed captions in war room videos. Ensure keyboard navigation works for all tools.
Incident Command and Documentation

The incident commander is responsible for ensuring that the incident is documented thoroughly. This includes the timeline, the decisions, the action items, and the stakeholder updates. The documentation should be stored in a searchable repository and linked from the incident ticket. Good documentation makes the postmortem easier and helps future incident commanders learn from history.

items: Ensure the scribe documents the timeline in real time
Review the documentation at the end of the incident
Store documentation in a searchable repository
Link documentation from the incident ticket

data.text: Incident Command and Organizational Memory

Incident documentation should become part of the organizational memory. Publish postmortems in the engineering wiki, present them at all-hands, and reference them during onboarding. Over time, the collection of postmortems becomes a training resource that helps new engineers learn how to respond to incidents without experiencing them firsthand.

items: Publish postmortems in the engineering wiki
Present interesting incidents at engineering all-hands
Maintain an incident search index for quick reference

data.text: Incident Command and Continuous Improvement

Every incident is an opportunity to improve the incident command process itself. After the postmortem, the team should ask: did our communication work? Did our decision framework help? Did our tooling support the commander? Use the answers to update the incident response plan, the runbook, and the training curriculum.

data.title: Process Improvement
data.text: After every SEV-1, hold a 30-minute process retrospective. What worked? What did not? Update the incident response plan based on the findings.
Incident Command and Organizational Culture

The way an organization handles incidents reveals its culture. A blameless, learning-oriented culture produces honest postmortems and continuous improvement. A blame-oriented culture produces cover-ups and repeated incidents. As a senior engineer, model the behavior you want to see: declare incidents early, participate fully in postmortems, and credit your team.
Culture is not what you say. It is what you do when the system is on fire.
Incident Command and Career Growth

Incident command is a leadership skill that distinguishes senior engineers from junior engineers. It demonstrates the ability to think clearly under pressure, communicate effectively, and make decisions that affect the business. Include incident command experience in promotion packets and performance reviews. Celebrate engineers who excel at incident command.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: The incident commander owns the process, not the technical details.
Clear roles prevent chaos during high-pressure incidents.
Communication should be timely, accurate, and empathetic.
Use decision frameworks such as OODA to act quickly under pressure.
Document every decision and action in the incident timeline.
Treat every incident as an opportunity to improve the process.
data.takeaway: Great incident commanders turn chaos into coordinated action and build trust through clear communication.

items.question: Who should be the incident commander?
items.answer: The most experienced on-call engineer for the affected service, or the engineering manager if the incident spans multiple teams.

items.question: What is the most important skill for an incident commander?
items.answer: Clear communication under pressure. Technical skills are secondary to the ability to coordinate and inform.

items.question: How do I delegate during an incident?
items.answer: Assign the technical lead, communications lead, and scribe at the start. Trust them to execute. Check in regularly but do not micromanage.

items.question: What if the incident commander makes a wrong decision?
items.answer: Correct it quickly and move on. Blame is not productive. Focus on the next decision.

items.question: How do I handle a long incident?
items.answer: Rotate the commander role every four hours. Take breaks. Delegate non-critical decisions. Maintain team morale.
